INTRODUCTORY REMARKS .
[OF COMMISSIONERS BULLOCK , NESBIT , AND CRADDOCK .]
We have concluded that itmight be interestingto the general reader
to have a shorthistoryof the Great Charter.
Magna Charta, or the Great Charterof Liberty, was, by the united
effortsofthenobility,clergy,and commonalty of England,wrestedfrom
King John, one of the most unscrupulous,tyrannical,and treacherous,
but,at the same time pusillanimoussovereigns, everon a throne. Of
the greatactorsin thatscene, itwas, in 1770, saidby Lord Chatham ,
in the House of Peers: " Their virtueswere rude and uncultivated, but
they were great and sincere. Their understandingswere as littlepol-
ished as theirmanners , but they had hearts to distinguishright from
wrong . They had heads to distinguishtruth from falsehood. They
understoodthe rightsof humanity, and they had the spiritto maintain
them ."
The Charter was granted to a congress of Barons , convened at Run-
nymede , which is saidby Leland , the great antiquary, to have been so
calledfrom two Saxon words signifyingthe " Council Meadow ," the
same having been used in old Saxon times as a place of Assembly .
The CharterbearsdateJune 15th, 1215,being one hundred and forty-
nine years afterthe Norman Conquest .
The copy we now present isnot that of the Charter having the royal
sealof John . That monarch died soon afterthe grant of Magna Charta,
and his infant son, Henry III, was crowned as his successor. It was
thought expedient by the Earl of Pembroke , Protectorof the Kingdom ,
and whose name isthe firstof the Barons appended to John's Charter,
that Magna Charta should be renewed by him . History informs us that
as oftenas fivetimes, during the reign of Henry , the Charter was rati-
fiedand confirmed. The form in which it now appears isthat given to
itin the ninth year of Henry III, and the same in which itappears at
thehead of the StatuteBooks of England. It is printedfrom the in-
speximus, and confirmationof itby Edward the First.
For a fullcomment on itsmost importantpassages, and forexplana-
tory notes, the reader is referredto the very interestingand instructive
work of ProfessorE. S. CREASY , entitled" The Rise and Progress of
the English Constitution." - EDITORS .

classification.summary: This statute outlines the conditions and procedures for removing a lawsuit from a state court to a federal circuit court. It specifies that removal is permitted when a suit is between a citizen of the state and a citizen of another state, and the latter petitions for removal due to a belief that they cannot obtain justice in the state court because of prejudice or local influence. The petitioner must provide surety for entering copies of the case proceedings in the federal court. The state court must then cease proceedings against the petitioner, and the case will proceed in the federal court as if originally brought there.

It focuses on diversity of citizenship and the potential for prejudice or local influence as grounds for removal. There is no mention of race, and the provisions apply to any citizen of another state, regardless of their race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'civil_laws' because it pertains to civil procedure and court processes.

It also lists several acts previously held to be constitutional, even though they dispensed with jury trials in specific civil and administrative contexts. classification.title: Change of Venue
classification.summary: This statute outlines the procedures and conditions for changing the venue of a legal case within Kentucky. It specifies that a change of venue must be made to an adjacent county that is most convenient to the parties, witnesses, and attorneys, and to which there is no valid objection. The order for change of venue is void if the party obtaining it does not pay the clerk a sum sufficient to cover travel expenses within ten days. The clerk is responsible for preparing and transferring the case record. The case will stand for trial at the next term if the papers are transferred ten days prior, otherwise, it will be tried at the subsequent term. Parties can also agree to a change of venue to any other court, regardless of adjacency.

It clarifies that when a defendant requests a continuance based on the absence of a material witness, the Commonwealth's attorney is not compelled to admit the truth of the witness's expected testimony. The Commonwealth can still present evidence to controvert the statements or impeach the absent witness. The court retains discretion to grant a continuance if justice requires it, unless the Commonwealth admits the truth of the alleged testimony. A provision is also made that these rules do not apply to motions for continuance made at the same term as the indictment. The statute also repeals conflicting acts and states its effective date.

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1887 outlines rules for deeds and conveyances of property. It defines general and special warranties in deeds, and specifies that deeds for land longer than five years, and marriage agreements, must be acknowledged or proved and lodged for record to be valid against purchasers for value without notice or creditors. It also states that deeds, mortgages, and other instruments required to be recorded must be recorded in the county clerk's office where the property is located to be effectual against purchasers without notice or creditors. Deeds of trust and mortgages are not valid against purchasers for value without notice or creditors until acknowledged or proved and lodged for record.

classification.summary: This section of the 1887 Kentucky General Statutes, specifically page 379, details various aspects of court jurisdiction. classification.title: Jurisdiction in civil matters for Justices of the Peace

It specifies that they have exclusive jurisdiction, concurrent with quarterly courts, over actions for the recovery of money or personal property where the matter in controversy does not exceed fifty dollars in value, and in other cases specifically provided by statute. It also details their powers to issue process, subpoena witnesses, and administer oaths. A footnote references an act from 1874 that expanded the jurisdiction of Justices of the Peace in certain counties to one hundred dollars, concurrent with circuit and quarterly courts, and details pleading requirements and taxes for claims exceeding fifty dollars. The footnotes discuss expansions of jurisdiction and procedural details but do not introduce any racial components. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Larceny, &c.
classification.summary: This statute defines grand larceny (value of $4 or more) and petty larceny (value less than $4). For grand larceny, the punishment is penitentiary confinement for one to five years. For petty larceny, persons other than females are punished by county jail confinement for one to twelve months, or hard labor for the same period. The court can assign such culprits to labor on county roads, streets, public buildings, or in a workhouse, under the control of the jailer, chained with a 50-pound ball, and not laboring more than eight hours a day. When not laboring, they are confined in jail.

classification.title: An Act to further regulate the retail traffic in spirituous, vinous, and malt liquors and nostrums used as a beverage.
classification.summary: This act requires druggists to obtain a license from the county court to sell spirituous, vinous, or malt liquors, or any nostrum containing alcohol used as a beverage, in any county, town, district, or place where such retail traffic is prohibited by law. The applicant must provide ten days' written notice to the county attorney and post similar notices publicly. Upon proof of notice and good character, and if the applicant is a bona fide dealer in drugs and medicines, a license may be granted for one year. Property to which the Commonwealth is entitled may be sold by the agent under the Auditor's direction.

classification.title: An Act concerning executors and administrators. / An Act providing for erecting at the graves of certain deceased persons memorial tablets, and providing a mode of paying for same.
classification.summary: This document contains two separate acts. The first act, approved March 6, 1876, allows courts of equity to grant executors, administrators, or curators a greater compensation than legally allowed (up to five percent) for insolvent estates, with the consent of the majority of creditors in amount. It also allows courts to authorize the compromise of bad or doubtful debts or claims of an estate. The second act, approved May 17, 1886, permits personal representatives or heirs of a decedent to erect memorial tablets at the grave, with the cost to be allowed as funeral expenses on the estate's settlement.

The first act (Ch. 39, § 1-3) concerns the administration of insolvent estates, specifically regarding executor compensation and the compromise of debts. The second act (II. § 1-2) pertains to the erection of memorial tablets at graves and their inclusion as funeral expenses. Neither of these acts mentions race, nor do they contain any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. They are administrative and procedural in nature, related to estate settlement and burial customs. Therefore, they are not Jim Crow laws.

Finally, it states that a conveyance of land will not be set aside as fraudulent unless the vendee had notice of the fraudulent intent.

classification.title: FRAUDULENT CONVEYANCES AND DEVISES
classification.summary: This statute addresses fraudulent conveyances and devises, specifically concerning pretended loans of personal property. It establishes that if personal property is loaned and remains in the possession of the borrower for five years without demand or legal action by the lender, the absolute right to the property is deemed to be with the possessor, favoring purchasers without notice or creditors. This presumption holds unless the written evidence of the loan, reservation, or limitation is recorded in the county of residence before possession is taken, or is contained in a properly recorded will. The statute also clarifies that a father holding possession of property gifted to his infant child acts as a natural guardian, and his possession is considered the child's, protecting the property from the father's creditors. It further defines possession for the statute of frauds as ostensibly by the debtor or for their use.

classification.title: An Act to Amend Chapter 46 of the General Statutes, Relating to Game and Small Birds
classification.summary: This act prohibits the catching, killing, or possession of doves between February 1st and August 1st, with a penalty of three dollars per offense. It also prohibits the taking of various song and insectivorous birds (night-hawk, whippoorwill, sparrow, thrush, lark, finch, marten, swallow, woodpecker, flicker, robin, oriole, red-bird, cedar-bird, tanager, cat-bird, blue-bird) at any time, unless they are destructive to crops, also with a three-dollar penalty. Robbing or destroying nests or eggs of wild birds is prohibited with a five-dollar penalty, except for predatory birds. Possession of protected animals or birds during prohibited periods is prima facie evidence of unlawful taking. Selling protected animals or birds during prohibited periods incurs the same penalty as unlawful taking. Each offense is distinct. Trapping, snaring, or netting protected animals or birds is prohibited with a three-dollar penalty per animal/bird. Trespassing for hunting is also mentioned.

classification.summary: This statute section outlines the legal rights and conditions related to curtesy (a husband's right to his deceased wife's property) and dower (a wife's right to her deceased husband's property). It details when a husband is entitled to curtesy, such as when he was actually seized of the wife's land or when rent was received. It also specifies conditions under which curtesy is not granted, like in cases of divorce or when land is held in trust. The statute then addresses dower rights, stating a widow is entitled to one-third of her husband's real estate, unless her right was barred, forfeited, or relinquished. It also touches upon a widow's rights concerning her husband's will and the sale of her dower interest.

classification.title: Attornment of Tenant and Conveyance of Land
classification.summary: This statute addresses the legal implications of a tenant's attornment (acknowledgment of a new landlord) and the effect of deeds that purport to convey more than the grantor lawfully possesses. It clarifies that a tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless consented to by the landlord or ordered by a court. It also states that a conveyance of rent, reversion, or remainder is valid without tenant attornment, but tenants paying rent to the grantor before notice of conveyance are protected. Furthermore, deeds conveying more than the grantor can lawfully assure will operate to convey only what the grantor can lawfully convey. If such a deed includes a general warranty, heirs or devisees who have received property from the vendor are barred from recovery to the extent of the value of the property received.

classification.summary: This act outlines the process for recording and releasing liens associated with mortgages and deeds. It specifies that a blank space must be left after the record of a deed or mortgage for each note or obligation. Assignments of notes must be noted in this space by the assignor, attested by the clerk. When a note is paid or released, the legal holder, as indicated by the record, can release the lien by signing and having it attested by the clerk. Only the legal holder of the note, as shown by the record, is permitted to release the lien. Any release made in contravention of this section is void. The act also sets a clerk's fee of twenty-five cents for each assignment and release.

classification.summary: This chapter outlines the powers and rights of landlords and tenants regarding leases, rent recovery, waste, holding over, and termination of tenancy. It specifies that a tenant conveying a greater estate than they possess passes only the estate they lawfully can convey. It also states that assignment or transfer of a lease by a tenant at will, by sufferance, or for less than two years, without landlord consent, forfeits the tenancy. Tenants who fail to quit possession after notice, or refuse to deliver possession when their term expires or is demanded, are liable for double rent.

It specifies that such an action can only be brought within fifteen years after the right to institute it first accrued to the plaintiff or their predecessor in claim. Footnotes clarify that 'real property' includes easements of light and air and a widow's dower right, and that a widow can sue for dower assignment against the legal title holder.
classification.reasoning: The provided text is from Chapter 71 of the 1887 Kentucky Statutes, titled 'Limitation of Actions.' The specific section analyzed (Article I, Section 1) deals with the time limits for bringing lawsuits to recover real estate. There is no mention of race, racial classifications, or any provisions that would suggest discriminatory intent or application based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'session_laws' as it appears to be part of a compiled legislative session's acts. The confidence is high because the content is clearly about civil procedure and property law, with no racial elements.

classification.title: LIMITATION OF ACTIONS
classification.summary: This section of the statutes outlines rules regarding the limitation of actions, specifically focusing on adverse possession. It details how adverse possession can be changed by agreement, how possession under one claim does not extend beyond enclosures, and the inability of certain parties (trustees, agents, tenants, etc.) to convert their possession to hostile without notice. It also addresses situations where a conveyance purports to convey the whole estate, and when a person expecting a conveyance is considered a quasi-tenant. The statute further discusses limitations against reversioners, remaindermen, and executory devisees, and limitations concerning cestuis que trust. It clarifies that possession by a grantor after conveyance with a life estate agreement is not adverse, and that statutes do not run against a reversioner until a contingency happens. Finally, it states that if a trustee's right of action is barred by limitation, the equitable right of the cestui que trust is also defeated.

classification.title: Limitation of Actions
classification.summary: This statute outlines the rules for the limitation of actions, specifically concerning the recovery of real property. It addresses how adverse possession affects the right of entry and details provisions for individuals under disability (infants, married women, or those of unsound mind) at the time their right to bring an action first accrued. It specifies that such individuals have three years after the disability is removed to bring their action, but the disability must have existed when the right to action first accrued. It also clarifies that subsequent disabilities or disabilities of heirs do not extend the limitation period, and discusses how co-existing disabilities and joint rights of action are handled.

classification.title: Limitation of Actions - Heirs Under Disability
classification.summary: This statute discusses the legal principles surrounding the suspension of statutes of limitation for heirs who are under a disability when a right of action accrues. It analyzes historical English and Kentucky statutes, particularly the Act of 1796 and the Revised Statutes, to determine when a limitation period, once begun, continues to run against representatives even if they are under disability. The text clarifies that for actions concerning real property, the limitation would suspend for heirs under disability, but this suspension was not extended to devisees. The statute emphasizes that under the Revised Statutes and General Statutes, if limitation began to run against a person, it would continue to run against their heir, regardless of the heir's disability.

The statute also clarifies that mere claims do not preserve a right to bring an action.

classification.summary: This section of the statutes outlines limitations on actions, specifically addressing when the limitation period begins to run for the recovery of streets, alleys, public easements, and public roads. It also details the discharge of sureties from liability after a certain period without execution or suit. Article V states that limitations for towns and cities to recover public easements do not begin until written notice of adverse possession is given. Article VI states that sureties are discharged after seven years without execution on a judgment or decree, and sureties on judicial bonds are discharged unless suit is brought within seven years of the cause of action accruing.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the administration and patient management of lunatic asylums in Kentucky. It details the appointment of special auditors, exemptions for asylum officers and servants from certain civic duties, regulations regarding the reception of out-of-state patients to prevent overcrowding for in-state residents, conditions for admitting private patients and discharging patients (including those committed on criminal charges), provisions for discharged pauper patients, and the board rates for paying patients. It also specifies which types of patients may be received.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to the management of lunatic asylums and does not contain any provisions that explicitly or implicitly discriminate based on race. The focus is on the operational aspects of the asylums, patient admission and discharge criteria, and administrative procedures. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: POOR AND POOR-HOUSES
classification.summary: This statute outlines the regulations for handling paupers within Kentucky. It prohibits bringing paupers from other states or counties into a new county without familial relation, and establishes procedures for arrest, surety, and fines for offenders. The county court is empowered to purchase land, erect poor-houses, contract for improvements, and levy taxes to support the poor and pay staff. Commissioners are appointed to manage the poor-house and its residents, with the authority to compel able-bodied paupers to labor. A receiver is appointed to manage funds for the institution.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses the management of paupers and the establishment of poor-houses. It focuses on the financial and logistical aspects of providing for the indigent and preventing the burden of paupers from being shifted between counties or states. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The language is neutral and applies to all individuals classified as paupers. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: REVENUE AND TAXATION
classification.summary: This statute outlines property exemptions from taxation in Kentucky. It exempts property of the United States, the Commonwealth, certain personal property for family use (cattle, crops, poultry, provisions), property owned by counties, cities, and towns necessary for government functions, public schools, churches, charitable institutions, public libraries, and property maintained by state taxation. It also clarifies that property used for gain or whose products are not solely devoted to charitable purposes is not exempt, and excludes property of insurance companies. Public libraries, paintings, and statuary owned by municipalities are also exempt.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with property tax exemptions and does not contain any language or provisions that suggest racial discrimination or segregation. It applies generally to all entities and individuals within the scope of the exemptions. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky General Statutes from 1887 outlines provisions for property taxation. It details how real estate should be listed for taxation, specifying that it should be listed in the county and tax district where it is situated against the owner of the first freehold estate. It also grants assessors the power to swear witnesses to ascertain ownership if the owner fails to list the property. The statute clarifies that tenants for a term of years are not liable for taxes, but tenants for life are. Leaseholds are to be listed as personalty, not real estate. It details how tuition fees are handled when students attend schools outside their designated district and specifies that cities or towns maintaining adequate common schools are considered single districts entitled to their proportion of the school fund. These city/town schools are to be managed by local authorities, with the county superintendent having no control over them. The statute also mandates that these city/town schools take a census of white children and report it to the county superintendent, with penalties for neglect.
classification.reasoning: The statute discusses the organization and management of public schools in Kentucky. While it does not explicitly mention race, the phrase 'census of the white children therein' indicates a racial distinction in the reporting requirements for schools in cities and towns. This implicit segregation in data collection and reporting, even if not directly about separate schools, is a characteristic of Jim Crow era legislation that often involved racial categorization in various aspects of public life. Therefore, it is classified as 'no' for being a direct Jim Crow law but has an implicit racial indicator due to the mention of 'white children'.

It outlines the funding mechanisms for these schools, which are derived from taxes specifically levied on colored persons, including property taxes, capitation taxes, dog taxes, taxes on deeds, suits, and licenses, as well as fines and penalties collected from colored persons. The statute also specifies that the per-pupil apportionment from federal land distribution funds for colored pupils shall not exceed that of white pupils.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly establishes a separate system of common schools for 'colored children.' This is a clear indicator of racial segregation in education, a hallmark of Jim Crow laws. The funding mechanisms are also derived from taxes levied specifically on colored persons, further reinforcing the discriminatory nature of the statute. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it is presented as part of 'The General Statutes of Kentucky-1887', which implies a compilation of laws.

It details the responsibilities of county commissioners in laying out school districts for colored children, specifying pupil age ranges and district sizes. It also covers the appointment of colored school trustees, their duties in managing schools, employing teachers, and notifying parents. The statute mandates a minimum school term length, with provisions for shorter terms under certain conditions. It also outlines the process for obtaining sites and erecting schoolhouses, and sets qualifications for teachers of colored schools, which are less stringent than those for white schools.

classification.title: VAGRANTS
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for dealing with convicted vagrants. Adults can be bound out to labor or sold into servitude for up to twelve months. Minors are to be apprenticed to learn a trade until they are twenty-one. The court is to pay prosecution fees and expenses from money received, then apply the remainder to the debts of the vagrant, and any remaining sum is to be paid to the wife and children, or the convict upon expiration of their term. Convicted vagrants with a wife and family have the right to enter into bond to return to and support their family.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses vagrancy and mandates that convicted individuals, particularly adults, can be 'bound out to labor' or 'sold into servitude' for a period not exceeding twelve months. This practice, especially in the post-Reconstruction South, was a common mechanism used to control and exploit Black labor. While race is not explicitly mentioned, the historical context of vagrancy laws during the Jim Crow era strongly suggests an implicit racial dimension, as these laws were disproportionately applied to Black individuals to circumvent the abolition of slavery and maintain a cheap labor force. The statute's focus on labor, servitude, and the potential for debt collection further aligns with the economic underpinnings of Jim Crow. classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky General Statutes from 1887, specifically Chapter 113 concerning Wills, outlines several provisions related to the validity and interpretation of wills. It addresses the competency of witnesses, particularly creditors, and their spouses, when the estate is charged with debts. It also clarifies that executors are competent witnesses and establishes rules for how wills are construed regarding the time they take effect and the disposition of after-acquired property. Furthermore, it details how provisions or advancements made to beneficiaries are to be treated as satisfaction of prior devises or bequests, especially in relation to children of the testator, and addresses the scenario where a devisee or legatee dies before the testator, leaving issue.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text pertains to the legal framework surrounding wills, including witness competency, the interpretation of will execution dates, and the handling of advancements and bequests. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it is part of a compilation of statutes, 'The General Statutes of Kentucky'.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for appealing the probate of a will to the circuit court, including the right to a jury trial. It also details provisions for non-residents and infants to challenge a will's probate within specific timeframes after a final decision. The county court can probate wills without a jury. The statute clarifies that proceedings to impeach a will's decision do not affect the rights of other interested parties, except for infants and non-residents. It also specifies that evidence taken during the initial probate motion can be used in subsequent trials if witnesses cannot be produced.

The mortgages must be worth at least double the amount loaned and be for a minimum of $20,000. The act also details the process for serving notice to the mortgagor about the transfer of the mortgage.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details regulations for life insurance companies regarding the deposit of securities. It outlines financial requirements and procedural steps for these deposits. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'session_laws' because it refers to an 'Act' passed on a specific date and mentions repealing inconsistent laws, which is characteristic of legislative session acts.

classification.summary: This act amends a previous act regulating public grain warehouses by repealing and substituting sections 10, 11, and 12. The substituted sections require warehousemen to post statements of grain on hand, receipts, deliveries, and issued/canceled receipts weekly. They also allow warehousemen to appoint an inspector and weigher, who must file a bond, or act as their own inspector and weigher. Warehousemen must also publish their storage and inspection rates monthly. This act takes effect upon passage but excludes warehouses within the corporate limits of Louisville.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the regulation of public grain warehouses, including requirements for posting statements, appointing inspectors and weighers, and publishing rates. It explicitly states that it does not apply to warehouses within the city of Louisville. However, there is no mention of race or any provisions that would inherently discriminate based on race. The exclusion of Louisville might be for other regulatory reasons not related to race. Therefore, it is classified as not a Jim Crow law.
